I have been farming these 7 mu in Quzhou for 45 years, and at 60 years old, I know every corner of my land. With just my wife and me at home now, I have to be careful with labor, but I am not about to give up the crops that have kept us fed and paid for our son's schooling. My main system is still wheat-maize double cropping—that is my insurance policy. I will put 4 mu into wheat-maize this year because that combination gives me grain for eating and steady cash from selling the surplus. The soil on those plots is decent, and I have my own well, so I can irrigate when the dry spells hit.

For the remaining 3 mu, I keep 1.5 mu of cotton because the price has been acceptable the last couple of years, and I know how to manage it. Yes, it needs more pesticide sprays and hand-picking labor, but I space them out and do most of the spraying myself. I also keep 1 mu of mungbean and 0.5 mu of red bean. The beans do not need much fertilizer—they fix their own nitrogen, which helps the soil—and my wife likes to cook with them. We sell a little at the village market too.

For wheat, I will rotary-till before sowing in early October and use an improved variety like the ones my neighbors have been planting. I will put down compound fertilizer as base and topdress with urea at jointing. Four irrigations should be enough: winter irrigation, then one at green-up, one at jointing, and one at grain filling. I expect about 450 kg per mu if the spring does not turn too dry.

For summer maize, there is no time for tillage after wheat harvest in mid-June, so I will plant directly into the wheat stubble—no-tillage, same as everyone else down the road. I will buy hybrid seed; it costs more, but the yield is worth it. Two irrigations are usually sufficient for maize here, one at the V6 stage and one at tasseling.

For cotton, I will rotary-till in April and plant an improved variety. Cotton bollworm is always a threat, so I will spray about 12 times through the season. I will irrigate twice, once at flowering and once at boll formation.

For mungbean and red bean, I will rotary-till the small plots and plant traditional seed I saved from last year. They only need one irrigation and minimal pesticide. I do not expect miracles from these small plots—maybe 90 to 110 kg per mu—but they cost almost nothing to grow and keep the rotation healthy.

I am a bit conservative with fertilizer because prices keep climbing, but I also know that cutting back too much on the wheat and cotton would hurt me more than saving a few yuan. So I stick to what the extension agent told me years ago, adjusted by what my eyes tell me when I walk the fields.
